KEY MESSAGE 1...Cool and unsettled through the weekend with periods 
of lake enhanced rain showers.

A well defined mid level closed low will cross NY/PA today before 
reaching New England tonight. The associated surface low will weaken 
over the eastern Great Lakes today, giving way to secondary coastal 
cyclogenesis along the New England coast. The resulting coastal low 
will deepen as it moves from the Gulf of Maine tonight to the 
Canadian Maritimes by Sunday.

Strongly diffluent mid/upper level flow ahead of the closed low atop 
low level frontogenesis and convergence will continue to support an 
area of rain across Central NY today, gradually moving north and 
east across the North Country and Saint Lawrence Valley as the 
closed low moves east. Rain will persist much of the day in these 
areas as the best synoptic scale forcing pivots overhead. 

Farther west, lake effect showers will continue this morning east of 
Lake Erie in convergent southwesterly flow just ahead of the closed 
low. The most persistent showers will be found along the Lake Erie 
shore through mid morning, with the northern extent occasionally 
reaching the Buffalo Metro area. There may be a few brief heavy 
downpours along the immediate lakeshore. The lake effect showers 
will tend to break up and weaken later this morning through the 
afternoon as the mid level closed low moves overhead and shear 
increases in the boundary layer.

Cool northwest flow will become established by early this evening as 
the coastal low deepens off the New England coast. Deep wrap around 
moisture on the western flank of the closed low will combine with 
lake induced instability and northwest upslope flow to support 
fairly widespread showers and light rain, peaking in coverage this 
evening through the early overnight. Boundary layer and surface 
temperatures will stay warm enough for all liquid, even across 
higher terrain. The deep moisture will quickly pull away late 
tonight through Sunday morning, with showers ending from west to 
east. The last of the showers across Central NY should end by mid 
morning Sunday.

Another progressive mid level closed circulation will dive southeast 
across Ontario and Quebec late Sunday through Monday morning. 
Increasing moisture and synoptic scale ascent will combine with lake 
induced instability to support another round of rain showers 
developing Sunday evening and lasting through Monday morning. The 
lake enhancement will initially be found east of the lakes Sunday 
evening in westerly flow, moving southeast of the lakes overnight 
through Monday morning as boundary layer flow veers to the 
northwest. Boundary layer temperatures will continue to support all 
liquid. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Windy Sunday, especially across Western NY.

A tight pressure gradient will persist Sunday across the Great Lakes 
ahead of a potent and fast moving mid level closed low. Forecast 
BUFKIT soundings show 40-45 knots of flow in the boundary layer 
Sunday afternoon, with adequate low level lapse rates to support 
mixing of stronger winds aloft to the surface. The strongest winds 
will be found across the Niagara Frontier northeast of Lake Erie, 
where gusts will reach or exceed 40 mph at a minimum. There is some 
potential for a few hours of near 50 mph gusts during the time of 
peak mixing in the afternoon. A Wind Advisory may eventually be 
needed if it appears these higher gusts will be realized. Gusts 
across the remainder of the area will be in the 25-35 mph range. 
Winds will diminish Sunday night as boundary layer flow veers to the 
northwest and the strongest winds aloft exit.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Somewhat milder weather returns early next week, 
followed by colder temperatures by the end of next week.

The pattern will become less active late Monday through the middle 
of next week as a WNW zonal flow develops across the northern tier 
of the CONUS. Dry weather will prevail much of the time, although 
shortwaves passing just north of the area combined with weak lake 
induced instability may support a chance of a few scattered showers 
at times, especially across the North Country. Temperatures will 
trend back to a little above average Tuesday through Wednesday.

The pattern will become more active again by the end of next week as 
a deep trough carves out over the Great Lakes and Northeast, 
evolving into a slow moving closed low by Friday and Saturday. In a 
general sense, this will bring a trend towards colder temperatures 
by the end of next week along with increasing chances for some rain 
and wet snow. There have been several individual deterministic model 
runs showing a stronger surface low and potential for an early 
season accumulating snowfall by Friday and Saturday. While such an 
event is within the realm of possibility, the airmass is not 
particularly cold and medium range models often show a cold bias at
